explanation: Fires on a token that comes right after a word that strongly sets up a fixed continuation (e.g. 'is [going]', 'an [well]-accepted', 'stop [of] course', 'usually [stick]', 'also [part]', 'is [based]'). It is strongest when the token is ungrammatical, misspelled or unexpected there ('is there [there]', 'an well', 'stop of course', 'I changes', 'behalf on'). This looks like a surprise or odd-continuation signal with no shared token identity.

Fires on tokens inside technical or formal named terms and identifiers: the second part of named psychometric instruments ('Brief Symptom [Inventory]', 'Anger [Scale]', 'rating [scale]'), legal reporter abbreviations ('Cal[.App]', 'Ill.[ App]', 'N.J.[ Super]'), compiler error codes ('CS[0]246'), PHP 'protected [$]', and the endings of scientific words ('first-pr[inciple]', 'immunosenesc[ence]'). The examples are a mix of reference and terminology contexts with no single theme.

Fires on varied function words, punctuation and word pieces in many genres (commas after 'say', 'the', 'of', 'who', 'in', subword continuations like 'sup[ine]', 'br[ukes]', 'C[ult]uring'). I can't find a common token or context.

Mixture. (1) 'as' in the comparison pattern 'as ADJ [as]' and 'beautiful [as] well'. (2) Boilerplate fixed phrases in code headers ('Code generated [by]', 'Licensed [under]'). (3) Code syntax tokens ('rgb[(]', 'Route[ path]', '$(', 'long[_description]'). (4) The middle subword pieces of chemical or foreign words ('amin[es]', 'se[ps]is', 'isosulf[an]', 'plural[idad]'). Each of these is predictable from the preceding context, but they don't share one job.

Fires on assorted highly predictable continuation tokens: ' use' inside a PHP class trait, '.com' after pastebin, 'See [the] License' in Apache headers, citation markers '@[B]4', 'better and [better]' or 'higher and [higher]', and journal-name completions ('Card[iology]', 'Catalog[ing]'). The one loose shared feature is that the token is nearly forced by the context, but the contexts have nothing in common.

Fires on the first function word or punctuation right after the opening noun phrase of a document or title, e.g. 'Amino acid substitutions [in]', 'Insecticide interaction [with]', 'How [do]', 'Riyadh, Saudi Arabia [--]', 'Walleye Warrior[:]', 'There's [a]'. It is strongest at the start of a title or abstract. The same words later in running text give weak or no activation.

Fires on the boundary token that ends a title, question or abstract and leads into the body: '?

' after a Q&A question title, '.'
' closing an arXiv abstract string before 'author:', '{
' opening a block, or 'How' starting the body. It is moderate on other line or statement boundaries in code.

Fires mainly on '.com' in website domains (medium.com, youtube.com, oup.com), and also on internet brand or platform names (Youtube, Reddit, Twitter) and e-commerce words ('Coupon', 'Rewards'). Weaker activations come from email headers ('Forwarded by') and API object names ('gapi.auth'). The overall theme is web, online-platform and commerce vocabulary.

Fires on tokens in fixed boilerplate or syntax that open a quoted key or argument, e.g. $_POST['  (the "[\'" token), meta name=" , \\usepackage{ , 'a copy [of] the License', 'relates [to]', HKEY. It also fires on some scientific word fragments ('dibenzo', 'Child-Pugh', 'type Ia'). The main job is opening a string or key in code or templates, mixed with unrelated license and science pieces.

Fires on the assignment or definition operator in math and code: '=' or 'be' after a variable in 'Let f = ...' or 'Let b be ...', '\\hat\\beta =', 'var max =', 'A =', and LaTeX openers such as '\\left(' and '{' in fractions. Weaker activations come from other structural tokens in code or text.

Activations are weak and varied apart from the top one. The strongest is 'public [key]' and '-key' in SSH or crypto contexts. Moderate ones include 'new' before a product or project ('Google's new Pixel'), domain nouns ('autism', 'expansion', 'Dermal') and verbs of learning or development. There is no coherent theme beyond the 'key' examples.

Fires on adjectives or adverbs of nearness or position that need a following complement, mainly 'close' ('close to', 'in close proximity', 'closely related', 'Close to 10'), plus 'early' ('early in life', the 'Early life' heading), 'different', 'important', 'all over'. It also fires on some unrelated subword pieces of Spanish or Portuguese words and names ('parado[ja]', 'Ir[win]').

Fires on adjective-forming suffixes or adjectives in scientific and academic prose, such as '-al', '-ological', '-ic', '-ural', '-istic', '-ometric', 'surgical', 'regulatory', 'constitutional', 'educational'. These are relational adjectives that modify a following noun ('transcriptional level', 'sociological perspective'). Plain adjectives in casual text are weak.

Fires on middle subword pieces of words split into several tokens, especially biochemical ones ('apol[ipop]rotein', 'Lip[op]rotein', 'vas[op]ressin', 'fluoro[quin]olone'). It also fires on identifier pieces in code ('HOM[EP]ATH', '.new', '_W') and on capital-letter word starts ('[C]inderella', '[MS] Access', 'best'+'seller'). The common thread is a token that is a fragment of a longer word, but the examples are heterogeneous.

Fires on distributive quantifiers, mainly 'each' and 'Each' (including the Danish 'Hver' and French 'Chaque'), and also 'every'. It fires moderately on 'per', on 'of' in 'each of', and weakly on 'everyone' and 'a day'.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word broken into fragments, especially 'pl' (plasmid, plasmon, plies, plumb, plazo, Plana) and 'og' (hypoglycemic, normoglycemia), and on initial consonant clusters of names or rare words ('fl'irty, 'Nor'carb, 'Cong'olese). The token is a word-initial or early fragment whose completion is predicted. It doesn't respond to the specific meaning.

Fires on a scattered set of tokens: prices after a price ('$35.95 [$]', '£288.3 [£]'), math variables after 'for' ('for [v]'), code fragments ('sd3[(x]', 'i <[ l]'), the 'A' in 'A:' answer headers, and bits of French words. No common feature.

Fires on the completion of proper-noun or fixed compounds: 'College' or 'University' after an institution's name, 'PRE[PROCESS]OR' macros, 'carbonic an[hydr]ase', 'res jud[ic]ata', 'Clack[mann]anshire', and 'at your [option]' in GPL headers. The common thread is the second or later part of a multi-token name, with educational institution names the strongest.

Fires in scientific or academic prose at the point just before a citation, number or list item: the citation bracket '\\[' or ' [@', the space before a number ('of [ ]10%', 'aged [ ]1 day'), commas in method lists ('chain reaction[,] western blotting'), and 'vs[.]'. This is a structural position in dense technical writing, usually right before a reference or a quantity.

Fires on the plural subject pronoun 'they' or 'They' when it refers back to a plural noun mentioned earlier ('cookies ... and [they]', 'so [they] can'). It also fires on plural noun subjects starting a clause ('Prebiotics', 'Tickets', 'articles') and, weakly, on 'we' and 'I' as subjects.

Fires on the first digit (or variable) right after a minus sign in math expressions, e.g. '-[1]0', '-[3]/4', '-[9]*o**3', '-[y]**2'. It is strongest in algebra problem text and weaker on digits after '-' in other contexts (version numbers, ranges, diff hunks '@@ -2912[,]').
